title: Nvidia Reports Nov. 17. History Says What Its Stock Usually Does Next. - The Motley Fool
content: The chipmaker has topped its own revenue forecast every quarter for over two years. So why have its shares dropped the next day more often than not? Nvidia (NVDA -1.26%) will report results for the three months ended Oct. 25 (its fiscal third quarter of 2027) after the close on Tuesday, Nov. 17. As of this writing, shares sit near $205, putting the stock about 14% under its Oct. 6 closing high of $239.24. Investors hoping a strong report can push the stock back toward its record might want to see how the artificial intelligence (AI) chip giant's shares have reacted lately. In all of Nvidia's past 10 reports, going back to May 2024, revenue beat the top of the range management had forecast. But the stock fell the next trading day after six of those. Still, I don't think this record is much of a reason to avoid the stock before the report. Because Nvidia's reports come out after trading ends for the day, the easiest way to gauge the move is from the report-day close to the next day's close. On that basis, the worst day of the stretch was in February 2025. The stock dropped around 8.5% after a fiscal fourth-quarter report with revenue up 78% year over year to $39.3 billion. That was almost $2 billion more than the $37.5 billion management had guided for. The pattern carried into 2026. Nvidia's revenue for its fiscal 2026 fourth quarter was $68.1 billion in February, over the company's $65.0 billion forecast, and shares dropped around 5% the next day. In May, fiscal first-quarter 2027 revenue of $81.6 billion beat a $78.0 billion forecast, and the stock dipped around 2%. With the drops after the August and November 2025 reports, that was four straight. Somebody is going to make a fortune on Anthropic’s IPO. It probably won’t be regular investors waiting for the day it goes public. Unless investors know where to look. Because two companies anyone can buy today already own pieces of Anthropic. And one of them owns a piece of OpenAI, too. Yet August's report snapped the streak. Revenue for the fiscal second quarter more than doubled, up 106% year over year to $96.2 billion, well above the $91.0 billion outlook. And the stock climbed around 9% the next day. Over all 10 reports, shares moved about 5% up or down on average. There's no simple pattern in which way they went, either. The February 2025 drop came with a forecast for Nvidia's gross margin to dip to 70.6% from 73%. But August's report also called for a lower gross margin (74%, down from 75%), and the stock climbed. Of course, the stock's other big gain in the stretch, around 9% in May 2024, followed the same report in which Nvidia announced a 10-for-1 stock split. For a long-term shareholder, what came after the first day counts more. Here, Nvidia's record looks far better. After five of the six drops, shares were back above their report-day close by the time Nvidia next reported, around three months later. After the February 2026 fall, for example, the stock rose about 21% from its post-report close by the May 20 report. The only exception was May 2026. Shares dipped around 2% the day after the report and were about 6% under their report-day close by the time the August report arrived. The record can go the other way, too. All of the 9% rise after August's report has since faded. As of this writing, shares are around 10% below where they closed the day after that report. Nvidia is guiding for fiscal third-quarter revenue of $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2%. If it hits the midpoint, revenue would climb around 89% from the $57.0 billion Nvidia pulled in for the same quarter last year. True, growth at that rate would be a slowdown from the 106% Nvidia posted in its fiscal second quarter. And shares could easily fall again on Nov. 18, the first trading day after the report. Going by the latest 10 reports, a drop is arguably a bit more likely than a rise. But the stock's valuation already looks reasonable. Analysts' consensus is for around $15.80 in earnings per share for fiscal 2028, which ends in January 2028. Using that figure, the stock trades at around 14 times earnings. That's a modest price for a company whose revenue more than doubled year over year in its latest quarter. So, does history say to wait for the report before buying? I don't think so. The day after has tilted negative. But most of those drops didn't last, and Nvidia has kept topping its own revenue forecasts. I'd consider buying shares before Nov. 17 rather than guessing the next day's move. title: Nvidia Stocks Rise 1.7% With Rubin Specification Gap Shifting Focus to Workload Tests - TradingView
content: Nvidia NVDA has a bandwidth question to answer behind its AI computing ambitions. Shares rose 1.68% to $208.08 at 10:00 a.m. ET on November 2, as Dataconomy's review highlighted differences between earlier Vera Rubin specifications and the current product table. For investors, the harder test is how much useful work customers get for their money. Nvidia's current Vera Rubin NVL72 specifications list memory bandwidth of 19.2 terabytes per second per GPU, versus up to 22 in its July 21 architecture bloga 12.7% difference. Memory capacity remains 288 gigabytes. Per-GPU NVLink bandwidth stands at 3 terabytes per second, compared with 3.6 previously, a 16.7% gap. Those comparisons do not establish equivalent slowdowns in customer workloads, and the November 2 coverage does not establish when the specifications changed. The GuruFocus snapshot gives Nvidia a GF Score of 96 out of 100, with strong profitability, growth and momentum readings, while valuation is its weakest dimension. That combination suggests business strength may already carry a demanding price tag. The bandwidth differences put more weight on delivered throughput, utilization and cost per token: those measures could show whether customers still earn compelling returns from the hardware. NVIDIA's growing AI reach does not remove the uncertainty in its valuation NVIDIA's October 7th 2026 RTX Spark announcement extends its AI platform into another part of computing. I see a strong business case, but a wide range of plausible values for the shares. At the October 9th 2026 close of $229.28, ValuationBot's October 11th 2026 base estimate of $281.22 is higher than the price. Its rating is still Hold because that estimate depends on demanding long-term assumptions. NVIDIA combines processors, networking, systems and software. Customers need working computing infrastructure, rather than an isolated component. Tools that help developers use the hardware can strengthen the relationship between product generations. RTX Spark brings the CUDA software platform to Windows laptops and compact desktops. NVIDIA said laptop preorders opened on October 7th, with availability from October 16th. This broadens the product opportunity, but an announcement does not establish sales, profitability or the size of a new market. The existing business provides much stronger financial evidence. NVIDIA reported fiscal second-quarter revenue of $96.2bn, up 106% from a year earlier. That scale supports the argument that AI infrastructure spending has become a large commercial activity. The challenge is deciding how long exceptional growth and profitability can persist. Forty per cent growth is a consequential assumption ValuationBot assumes 40% annual revenue growth for five years before tapering towards 4.5% mature growth over ten years. Five years at 40% would expand revenue to more than five times its starting level. This is a major allowance for adoption, rather than a restrained forecast of ordinary semiconductor growth. NVIDIA's integrated architecture and broad customer use make rapid expansion plausible. More computing demand can support sales across processors, networking and systems. However, equipment orders need power, facilities and customer funding before they become productive deployments. The model therefore carries substantial execution exposure. If customers cannot earn adequate returns on their infrastructure, future orders may slow even while demand for AI services grows. Competition and customer-designed accelerators could also change who receives the profit from that demand. A growing market does not guarantee an unchanged share of its economics. Lasting net profit matters more than headline margins The base case assumes a mature adjusted net margin of 55%. It recognises considerable pricing power and the ability to spread research across a large sales base. That margin is a model judgement about sustainable earnings, not company guidance. NVIDIA's latest quarter had a 75% gross margin. Gross margin precedes operating costs and tax, so it cannot be used directly as the profit available to shareholders. Reported earnings can also include investment gains that do not measure recurring product economics. The strongest business case is that software, system integration and continued product leadership preserve exceptional profit conversion. The constraint is that research, transitions between products, supply requirements and competition remain real costs. Evidence of recurring net earnings through several product generations would support the mature assumption more strongly than a single quarter. The valuation relies on capital and distant cash flows The model allows $2 of added revenue for each $1 of additional operating equity investment, with a mature return on equity of 45%. Outsourced manufacturing supports capital efficiency, but research, inventory and customer delivery still require resources. ValuationBot requires an initial shareholder return of about 23.5%, declining towards 11.8% at maturity. Supply-chain concentration and export exposure matter to that judgement. Lower required returns would increase value, while disruption would make the optimistic cash-flow path harder to deliver. Approximately 64% of the model's operating present value comes from the terminal period. Much of the answer therefore depends on economics well beyond the next earnings release. The strongest adverse evidence would be slowing repeat orders, pricing pressure or supply disruptions that turn committed capacity into an earnings burden. I would focus on those outcomes rather than interpret every product announcement as an equal addition to value. Nvidia invented the GPU, the chip behind nearly every major AI system on the planet. But it’s so much more today. It sells entire “AI factories” in a box: multi-rack systems packed with processors, memory, servers, cooling, and the high-speed networking that lets everything work together like one big “brain.” And its CUDA software is so deeply embedded across every cloud, AI lab, and frontier model that it’s become the de facto AI infrastructure operating system. Nvidia grew revenue 106% year over year from $46.7 billion to $96.2 billion in fiscal Q2 2027 (ended July 26, 2026). That’s unprecedented. No public company in history has ever organically doubled quarterly revenue from such a large base. Nvidia’s “Data Center” revenue, which is the AI business, grew 117% year over year in Q2 to $89 billion. The company guided for total revenue of $108 billion this quarter, which would be its first $100 billion quarter. It also guided for 70% revenue growth in fiscal 2028, which is basically calendar year 2027. And the cap on that growth guidance is supply, not demand. The company said it would have been about double again absent the supply crunch. Meanwhile, the customer list has broadened considerably. For two years, the most popular argument against Nvidia was basically: “Its whole business depends on four giant customers, all of which are building their own chips to become less reliant on Nvidia.” It’s true that these four “hyperscalers”—Amazon, Microsoft, Google (GOOGL), and Meta Platforms (META)—have been driving much of the AI infrastructure buildout. They’ll continue to do so for at least a few more years. And all four are indeed building their own AI chips these days. But as the hyperscalers have increased their AI spending, so have lots of other companies. Governments around the world have too for their “sovereign AI” initiatives. And we now have a lot more color on that broadening AI spending… In Q1, Nvidia started separating its AI revenue into two buckets. Bucket one is the hyperscalers. Bucket two is everybody else, which Nvidia calls ACIE (short for AI Clouds, Industrial, and Enterprise). So ACIE covers the neoclouds, governments, hospitals, banks, carmakers, drug companies, AI startups, etc. Meanwhile, most of the customers in the faster-growing ACIE bucket will never even think about designing their own chips. What’s more, the hyperscalers have shown no signs of pulling back yet. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress said it clearly on the call: “With cloud industry backlog now greater than $2 trillion, CapEx by the top five hyperscalers is expected to reach nearly $800 billion in 2026 and $1.3 trillion in 2027.” (Oracle is the fifth hyperscaler she referred to.) And Amazon—which does design its own AI chips and has basically been Exhibit A for the whole “hyperscalers will defect” thesis—committed to deploying another 2 million Nvidia GPUs through 2028. Amazon is also adopting Nvidia’s full physical AI stack (Omniverse, Cosmos, Isaac, and Jetson) to power its fleet of warehouse robots. So the giants are still buying from Nvidia, a new class of customer has shown up behind them, and both are compounding at once. First, the Vera Rubin ramp. Nvidia expects supply to stay tight through at least fiscal 2028 (basically calendar 2027). We want to see the company deliver at least the 70% growth it expects. I also want gross margin to bottom in the 71% to 72% range. If it falls below that threshold, it means memory costs are temporarily winning the tug-of-war Second, how much Nvidia invests in, guarantees, and backstops its customers. It has about $165 billion in these types of financing arrangements. Critics call this “circular financing.” But we’re not concerned. Those guarantees are only about 1.3X Nvidia’s trailing 12-month free cash flow… and only about half of our two-year forward annual free cash flow forecast. What’s more, if a customer fails, what’s left behind is Nvidia equipment that other buyers are lining up for, not dark fiber like after the dot-com bust. Third, the Open Agent Safety Platform Nvidia launched just this week. It’s a two-piece (hardware and software) system for keeping AI agents inside the boundaries set by operators. The launch follows disclosures from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google of recent incidents in which their AI models escaped their test sandboxes—during testing with safeguards reduced, I should add—and hacked other organizations. Nvidia says that from what it knows about the most notorious of such incidents—OpenAI’s models breaching Hugging Face—this new platform could have stopped it. The significance: Nvidia is basically trying to make its hardware the place where AI agent safety lives. And it’s giving away the software layer to make that architecture the industry default—the classic CUDA-style playbook applied to safety. It strengthens the “you need the whole Nvidia stack” narrative and gives CEO Jensen Huang a powerful talking point and a place at the table on one of the industry’s biggest problems. A Democratic House can’t undo an executive decision past a veto. So what can it reach? China can’t hurt Nvidia’s numbers much more. The power bill can. Nvidia shipped its first H200 chips to China in the quarter that ended in July. They were less than 1% of its $89 billion in data-center sales. Its forecast for the next quarter, $108 billion, counts no China data-center sales at all. On a normal trading day, Nvidia’s value moves by about $76 billion. One ordinary day is worth more than all of Nvidia’s China data-center sales last quarter. December 2025: the White House allowed H200 sales to approved Chinese buyers, with 25% of the revenue going to the U.S. government, up from 15% on the older H20 (as reported). Commerce published the license rules in January 2026. Beijing told its companies to shun the H20 and has been slow to approve H200 buying (as reported). Nvidia’s newest chips, Blackwell and Rubin, aren’t approved for China. Daily move: median daily move over the past year ≈ 1.5%, times $4.95 trillion ≈ $76 billion. China H200 sales: under 1% of $89 billion, so under $0.9 billion. Some would. China hawks in both parties dislike the H200 deal, and a Senate bill, the SAFE Act, would stop licenses for chips to China for at least 30 months. A Democratic House could hold hearings on the 25% cut and ask whether Washington should be taking a share of a company’s sales at all. The worst case for China is roughly what investors are told to expect. A hawkish House can’t take away revenue Nvidia isn’t counting. At the plug. AI runs on data centers, data centers run on power, and power bills are on the ballot. Electricity prices rose about 6.7% in 2025, and Goldman Sachs expected data centers to drive about 40% of the growth in demand. Ads mentioning data centers had cost over $45 million this year by August. Democrats are campaigning on it. So are many Republicans. That’s what makes it different. title: Prediction: Nvidia Stock Is Going to Soar After Nov. 17 - The Motley Fool
content: With hyperscalers' capital expenditures holding up, Nvidia has a lot working in its favor. Nvidia (NVDA -1.26%) has been one of the stock market's biggest winners over the last several years. Its market cap now tops $5 trillion, and the stock is still on the rise -- it's up nearly 15% in 2026 so far. Investors who bought the stock three years ago are sitting on a whopping 429% return. Stretch that timeline to five years, and Nvidia is up 759%. Those are outstanding returns, but I don't think Nvidia is finished rewarding shareholders. In fact, I believe it could have another big move coming after the chipmaker reports its fiscal 2027 third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17. Here's why I'm bullish on Nvidia stock heading into its next earnings report. It's difficult to appreciate just how quickly Nvidia is growing until you look at the numbers. The company generated $96.2 billion in revenue during its fiscal 2027 second quarter, which ended July 26. That was a 106% increase from the prior-year period, with data center revenue climbing 117% to $89 billion. And Nvidia is making an enormous amount of money on those sales. Its non-GAAP gross margin reached 75%, meaning Nvidia retained 75 cents of every revenue dollar after accounting for the direct costs of producing its products. Adjusted earnings per share increased 120% to $2.22. Those aren't the financial results of a company whose best days are necessarily behind it. For the fiscal third quarter, Nvidia is forecasting revenue of approximately $108 billion, representing another substantial increase from the $57 billion it generated a year earlier. Wall Street expects even more. According to Yahoo! Finance, analysts are projecting revenue of approximately $109 billion and adjusted earnings of $2.47 per share. That would amount to revenue growth of roughly 91% and earnings growth of 90% from the year-ago quarter. Nvidia has already demonstrated that it can deliver extraordinary growth even at its now enormous scale. Another strong quarter, particularly if management raises its outlook, could give investors another reason to push the stock higher. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been bullish about the company's future, and his confidence isn't limited to its potential to sell more graphics processing units (GPUs). Huang believes global spending on AI infrastructure could reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion by 2030. He has also indicated that Nvidia expects to sell twice as many chips in 2027 as it does in 2026. Earnings from big tech companies give Nvidia investors a lot to look forward to. Meta Platforms raised the low end of its 2026 capital spending range from $135 billion to $145 billion, Alphabet held its $195 billion to $205 billion capex budget range steady, and Microsoft trimmed its 2026 plan slightly from $175 billion to $170 billion. However, Alphabet also said it expects spending to rise significantly in 2027, and Microsoft's CFO said she expects spending to accelerate in the first half of 2027 on higher component costs and delayed deliveries. Amazon, which reported its latest results after the closing bell on Oct. 29, also reaffirmed its plan to spend $220 billion this year. As a group, hyperscalers are expected to spend more than $1 trillion on capex next year, and since these companies are among Nvidia's biggest customers, budgets that hold steady or rise support its demand picture heading into its report after the close on Nov. 17. But there's another part of Nvidia's growth story that I find particularly compelling. The company's next-generation Vera Rubin architecture is designed to deliver more computing power from each gigawatt of electricity it consumes. And Nvidia expects the platform to generate considerably more revenue for each gigawatt of computing capacity. Huang explained during the company's August earnings call that Nvidia's revenue opportunity increased from approximately $18 billion per gigawatt with its Grace Hopper platform to $25 billion with the Grace Blackwell platform that succeeded it in late 2024. With the new Vera Rubin platform, that figure could reach $40 billion. That's a 60% increase from Blackwell, without requiring its data center customers to add more electrical capacity. If customers continue buying Nvidia's increasingly sophisticated AI systems, the company has an opportunity to grow revenue at a faster rate than it grows its chip shipments. Despite its incredible stock performance, Nvidia trades at approximately 23 times forward earnings. That's a premium to the S&P 500's forward price-to-earnings ratio of 18.6, but I believe it's extremely reasonable given Nvidia's growth. Remember, analysts expect Nvidia's earnings to grow by approximately 95% during fiscal 2027. They're also forecasting another 71% increase in fiscal 2028. With Wall Street already expecting nearly $109 billion in quarterly revenue, Nvidia has a high bar to clear. Moreover, even an earnings beat doesn't guarantee a stock rally if investors are disappointed by management's guidance. But I'm not particularly worried about Nvidia's premium valuation. We're talking about a company that's more than doubling quarterly revenue, maintaining gross margins around 75%, and preparing to sell increasingly valuable AI computing systems. Paying 23 times forward earnings for that kind of performance doesn't strike me as excessive. But with AI infrastructure spending continuing, Nvidia's earnings growing rapidly, and its valuation looking reasonable relative to its prospects, I believe the odds favor another strong performance from Nvidia in its next earnings report. That's why I'm bullish on Nvidia heading into Nov. 17 -- and why I think shares could climb substantially afterward. Patrick Sanders has positions in Nvidia. title: NVDA Stock In For ‘Very, Very Fast’ Rally: Analysts Shrug Off Price-Hike Buzz Ahead Of Most-Watched Earnings Report - Stocktwits
content: Shares of Nvidia, Inc. (NVDA) rose nearly 1% in premarket trading on Tuesday, attempting to rebound from a seven-session rout as analysts argued that potential price increases for its newest AI systems should not derail demand and could strengthen an already bullish earnings setup. NVDA stock fell 3% on Monday but remains up 4% for August, putting it on track for its strongest monthly performance since May. Nvidia could reportedly raise prices for its Blackwell and Rubin systems as soaring memory costs push up production expenses. However, Raymond James analyst Simon Leopold said that a potential 15% increase would make sense given the amount of high-bandwidth memory packed into the platforms. “15% really doesn’t seem all that demanding,” Leopold said, adding that an even larger increase is possible. Each Blackwell and Rubin GPU is paired with eight HBM stacks, each containing 12 layers of DRAM. Nvidia has also spent years locking in memory supplies through long-term agreements with multiple suppliers, potentially cushioning the effect of rising costs. Still, Leopold cautioned that higher list prices may not translate directly into higher prices for major customers. “The public prices may go up by 15%, but that doesn’t mean contracted prices are reflecting that same amount,” he said. Wall Street is bracing for another enormous quarter from Nvidia on Wednesday. Fiscal.ai projects revenue of $91.48 billion, more than double the year-earlier figure, with adjusted earnings of $2.07 per share and EBITDA of $61.83 billion. Koyfin’s estimates are slightly higher at $92.07 billion in revenue, $2.09 in adjusted earnings and $61.99 billion in EBITDA. This would represent sequential growth of 13% in revenue and EBITDA and 12% in earnings. KeyBanc reiterated its ‘Overweight’ rating and $330 target, implying roughly 58% upside from Nvidia’s $208.48 close. “Expect ramping Rubin GPU shipments to drive strong results and guidance,” the firm said. R200 production began in July, with shipments expected to increase by about 250,000 units sequentially in the third quarter as Blackwell volumes remain flat. KeyBanc raised its full-year R200 estimate to roughly 1.9 million units, citing stronger HBM4 supply from SK Hynix, and called the risk-reward “favorable” at 15 times its fiscal 2028 earnings estimate. Meanwhile, Rosenblatt maintained a ‘Buy’ rating and $325 target, suggesting 56% upside. The firm expects Wednesday’s results and third-quarter guidance to beat consensus as Vera Rubin deployments accelerate. Cantor Fitzgerald offered the highest target at $350, implying nearly 68% upside from the last close, while reiterating its ‘Overweight’ rating. “Investors are underweight NVDA and when this stock starts moving, it is going to move very, very fast,” the firm said, keeping Nvidia as a Top Pick. Cantor sees additional catalysts in a clearer 2027 data-center outlook, sustained neocloud growth, hyperscaler spending visibility through 2028 and growing acceptance of GPUs as a new asset class. Morningstar expects Nvidia to comfortably beat its previous guidance and raise its outlook as hyperscalers continue investing heavily in AI infrastructure. It said long-term investors could begin with a small position before earnings while keeping “enough dry powder” to buy more on weakness. Notably, NYSE floor trader Jay Woods identified $195 and Nvidia’s previous closing peak near $235.74 as the levels to watch. From $208.48, the figures represent 6.5% downside and 13% upside, respectively. title: NVDA, AVGO’s AI Backstops Have One Analyst Worried — Michael Burry Says There’s A Reason Nvidia’s 5Y CDS Are Going ‘Parabolic’ - Stocktwits
content: Wolfe Research senior analyst Chris Caso said Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) and Broadcom Inc. (AVGO) are taking on a new source of long-term risk by backstopping financing for key AI customers. During an interview with CNBC, Caso expressed concern that this backstop strategy creates liabilities that leave him “less comfortable” even as it helps sustain the AI infrastructure spending boom. “That part of it is less good, because there's some liability on there. That liability is probably far in the future, but that part I'm less comfortable with,” he said. Nvidia shares were down 2% in Wednesday’s opening trade, while Broadcom shares were down about 0.4%. Caso said Nvidia's financial strength gives it the flexibility to take on financing commitments that few companies in the semiconductor industry could match. “Right now, the benefit Nvidia has is that they are generating just so much cash. They have such a strong balance sheet, and probably the healthiest balance sheet in the industry,” he said. Caso suggested the backstop strategy may reflect an effort to ensure financing doesn't become a constraint on AI infrastructure spending. “I think what Jensen's trying to do is figure that if financing becomes a bottleneck, that constrains his business, so let's try to remove that bottleneck,” Caso said, adding that Broadcom is pursuing a similar approach. Nvidia announced a partnership with the SK Group last week for a $500 billion initiative spanning AI factories and next-generation memory. The company is also in talks to backstop about $250 billion to help OpenAI lease compute for a data center project, according to a report by Bloomberg. Meanwhile, Broadcom announced a new AI XPV platform last month in partnership with Apollo and Blackstone’s Credit & Insurance Business, with an initial tranche of $35 billion. “The Big Short” investor Michael Burry turned his attention to Nvidia's credit risk. In a post on X, Burry wrote that there is a reason the chipmaker's five-year credit default swaps (CDS) are going “parabolic,” blaming what he described as Nvidia”s overreach to send “circular spending to biblical proportions.” Burry's remarks came alongside a chart showing a sharp rise in Nvidia's five-year CDS, financial contracts that act as insurance against a company's debt default. Caso, for his part, said Nvidia's financing commitments create long-term liabilities but acknowledged that the company's cash generation and healthy balance sheet give it ample capacity to shoulder those risks. title: History Says Now Is the Perfect Time to Buy Nvidia Stock - The Motley Fool
content: 2026 hasn't been the best year for Nvidia (NVDA -1.26%). While it's up 13% versus 11% from the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.51%), Nvidia investors don't expect market-beating performance; they expect market-crushing performance. When you look at Nvidia's results, it's easy to see it should be doing better, as it grew revenue at 106% in the second quarter (Q2). Over the long term, company growth and stock performance tend to be highly correlated, so what's up with the disconnect? I believe it's just the market lagging behind, and history tells us that right now is an incredible buying opportunity. The best way to value Nvidia from a current and historical perspective is to utilize the forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio. This metric uses analysts' estimates for the full fiscal year to price the stock, so it bakes in some growth. At the start of a fiscal year, these measures tend to look pretty cheap, as there is a full year's worth of growth ahead. When you get halfway through the fiscal year (Q3 results aren't available yet), this starts to become a more conservative estimate, as only six months of growth are projected. So, sometimes stocks start to look a tad expensive toward the end of the year. In both 2024 and 2025, Nvidia's stock reached 40 times forward earnings before the year was over. That's not the case this year. At just under 23 times forward earnings, Nvidia hasn't seen the end-of-year rally it normally does. This raises the question of why, and I think it's simply because the market is trying to call Nvidia's bluff (even if it's wrong). The S&P 500 trades at about 19.2 times forward earnings, so Nvidia trades at only a slight premium to the broader market. This is essentially the market conveying that after this year, it expects market-average growth from Nvidia. Somebody is going to make a fortune on Anthropic’s IPO. It probably won’t be regular investors waiting for the day it goes public. Unless investors know where to look. Because two companies anyone can buy today already own pieces of Anthropic. And one of them owns a piece of OpenAI, too. But according to Nvidia and Wall Street analysts, that's a gross error. Nvidia itself told investors during its Q2 earnings call that it expects 70% revenue growth next year. It's rare for a company to provide next-year guidance six months before the year begins, but it shows the confidence Nvidia has in its future growth. This is likely because many of its clients have locked in orders for next year, giving it high visibility of what's to come. Wall Street analysts are also bullish, expecting 68% revenue growth next fiscal year. All of this adds up to a company that will deliver excellent growth next year, which should result in huge returns. If we value Nvidia's stock using next fiscal year's estimates, the stock trades for just 13.3 times earnings. So, if Nvidia hits all projections and the stock doubles, that means it would only trade for 26 times trailing earnings. That's a reasonable price tag for a company of Nvidia's stature and pedigree, so expecting the stock to rise significantly over the next year isn't out of the question. As a result, I think the historical record is pretty clear that the future is bright for Nvidia. But that's just 2027. Beyond 2027, there's a broad expectation for the AI build-out to last through at least 2030, giving Nvidia even more time to capitalize on a generational growth opportunity. There are few better buys in the market than Nvidia right now, and investors shouldn't wait around too long; now is the time to strike. One of the liveliest ongoing debates on Wall Street is whether artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure spending will continue to grow at a good clip over the medium term. If it doesn't, some industry leaders will see revenue and earnings growth slow, and their share prices could sink. But if it does, some AI-focused companies still have plenty of room to run. Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), recently made comments that support the bullish outlook. Of course, Huang is hardly an unbiased observer. Still, it's worth paying attention to what he said and the potential implications for Nvidia and other AI leaders. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » First, a little bit of background on neocloud companies. Unlike traditional cloud computing providers like Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) that offer a broad range of services, neoclouds specialize in renting out the compute power needed to develop and run AI models. Neoclouds became more prominent as the AI revolution took off, but there is more room for them to grow, at least if we believe the words of Jensen Huang. In a recent interview, the CEO of Nvidia said: If you look at the fundamentals, the demand for the neoclouds is off the charts. Their capabilities are extraordinary, and so what is missing in the middle is the working capital to fuel that growth, to fund that growth. There is a lot to unpack here. First, the great news. Demand for neocloud services being off the charts is a bullish sign for Nvidia. These neoclouds purchase GPUs (graphics processing units) from the company and rent out GPU compute to other corporations. Growing demand could force these companies to expand their capacity. That means they may keep buying Nvidia's GPUs. But can they afford this massive AI build-out? That's the not-so-great news. As Huang pointed out, these companies may lack the capital necessary to purchase the infrastructure -- including GPUs -- to meet demand for their services. Recent developments support Huang's view. Companies like CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) and even Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ:SPCX) have said that there is more demand for their services than they can (or are willing to) provide, at least in the short term. Meanwhile, CoreWeave has raised more than $30 billion in debt and equity capital this year. Note that the company is worth about $33 billion as of writing, so it has raised capital equivalent to almost 91% of its market cap in a single year. That points to the financial bottleneck Huang mentioned and to how some neocloud companies are looking to solve it. But what does all this mean for Nvidia's prospects? One bullish scenario could go like this. CoreWeave and its neocloud peers will conjure up various ways to fund their massive AI build-outs. Perhaps they will borrow more, or resort to dilutive forms of financing (or both). Another possibility is that more competitors will enter the market upon seeing the massive, lucrative opportunity. The result: neocloud companies will continue to purchase the infrastructure necessary to meet demand for their services, and some of that money will flow directly into Nvidia's pockets. Of course, this also assumes that the AI boom will continue unabated at least over the next few years. If it doesn't, neoclouds could significantly reduce spending, leading to lower demand for Nvidia's products. Which scenario is more likely? Probably something closer to the first one. Soaring demand for neocloud services, the growing popularity of AI agents, and several other indicators support this. Medium-term projections for AI infrastructure spending remain high for these (and other) reasons. And Nvidia could be one of the biggest winners. So, it's not too late to invest in the stock, even after its amazing run in recent years. title: Here's What $10,000 Invested Equally in SpaceX and Nvidia Could Be Worth in 2030 - The Motley Fool
content: A $10,000 investment in SpaceX and Nvidia could rise fivefold by 2030. Nvidia (NVDA -1.26%) and Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +1.23%) are two of the most exciting artificial intelligence (AI) stocks, and with SpaceX deciding to build its data centers exclusively on Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform, the two companies are inextricably linked. With $10,000 split between the two stocks, investors could buy 34 shares of SpaceX and 23 shares of Nvidia. With SpaceX set to ramp up its compute capacity to levels never seen before, a $10,000 investment split between the two stocks could be worth over $52,000 by the end of 2030. Here's how. SpaceX has seen some of the best returns on its AI infrastructure investments, with a payback breakeven in about a year. Meanwhile, CEO Elon Musk thinks the company can push that down to around six months. With that type of return profile, SpaceX is set to embark on one of the largest AI infrastructure investments ever seen. Musk said the company plans to end this year with up to 3 gigawatts of computing power and end 2027 with at least 13 gigawatts. Meanwhile, it has a long-shot goal of adding up to an incremental 20 gigawatts of computing capacity next year. One gigawatt of power costs approximately $50 billion to build on Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform, so SpaceX is looking to spend at least $500 billion in capital expenditures (capex) next year on AI infrastructure, with the potential to spend up to $1 trillion. Meanwhile, Musk has projected that this could help SpaceX end 2027 with between $500 billion and $1 trillion in annual recurring revenue (ARR). Now, let's say SpaceX adds 10 gigawatts of compute capacity each of the next five years; that would give the company 53 gigawatts of computing power at the end of 2031. Assuming similar revenue per gigawatt, that would be a year-end 2031 ARR of around $2.65 trillion. Throw in SpaceX's Starlink, increased rocket launches, and AI coding growth, and it could hit $3 trillion in revenue in 2031. Place a 5 times price-to-sales (P/S) multiple on the stock, and it would be worth $15 trillion. However, all this capex will lead to a higher share count, which we'll assume will be diluted by 10% in 2027, gradually stepping down by 1% a year. This would lead to a $750 share price, and those 34 shares would be worth $25,500 by the end of 2030. Nvidia gets roughly $40 billion per gigawatt in revenue from its Vera Rubin architecture. This comes not only from its graphics processing units (GPUs), but also from its networking components, other chips -- such as central processing units (CPUs) and inference language processing units (LPUs) -- and its expanding software layer that goes into the configuration of its Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale supercomputing platform. As such, if SpaceX adds 10 gigawatts of power a year, it would equate to around $400 billion in annual revenue just from one customer. However, Nvidia obviously has a lot of customers and has been growing rapidly. Nvidia has also been able to get more revenue per gigawatt with each new generation of its architecture, going from approximately $18 billion for Hopper to $25 billion for Grace Blackwell, and now $40 billion with Vera Rubin. There is good reason to believe this will continue. As such, I think Nvidia's current analyst estimates will likely prove too low. If Nvidia can sell more Vera Rubin systems to SpaceX without missing out on selling capacity to other customers, its fiscal 2028 revenue could be closer to $850 billion. That would take my model to the company generating adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of nearly $61 in fiscal 2032 (ending January). Place a 19 times forward P/E on that, which is a current S&P 500 market multiple, and the stock would be worth $1,160 by the end of 2030. Meanwhile, those 23 shares would be worth roughly $26,650. However, growth slowed in 2025, with competitors such as Intel, Broadcom, and AMD delivering higher returns. This raises a key question for investors: should they continue to hold Nvidia shares, or is the stock overvalued, making it more prudent to explore undervalued opportunities? This review offers insights into whether to buy, hold, or sell Nvidia shares in 2026. Nvidia is one of the world's leading companies in the semiconductor sector. Its graphics processing units (GPUs) are used in robotics, cloud computing, neural network development, machine learning, and AI, as well as in automated systems. Over the past five years, Nvidia's stock has gained 1,325%, making it the world's largest company by market capitalization by the end of 2025, overtaking Apple. In 2025, NVIDIA delivered a stock return of 53.26%, lower than those of its main competitors: AMD, Broadcom, and Intel. For the next five years, the company has forged strategic partnerships with major tech firms such as Meta and Samsung, while investing billions of dollars in OpenAI and other innovative startups. NVDA shares are expected to continue appreciating, though likely at a more moderate pace. The stock remains suitable for diversifying a long-term investment portfolio. For Nvidia, the elevated P/E reflects expectations of growing demand for chips used in AI and data centers. Forward P/E: 16.51 – Significantly lower than the current P/E, this indicates that analysts expect a sharp increase in earnings. In this case, earnings growth is more than twice the pace of stock price growth, signaling strong expected earnings momentum in the coming years. Regarding other financial metrics, the company is outperforming the industry average by a significant margin. Is NVDA a good stock to buy? The answer depends on your investment goals. It is unlikely that you will be able to double your investment quickly, as the AI boom is largely behind us. However, Nvidia remains a leader in the development of graphics processors and artificial intelligence solutions. The company has long-term contracts with the world's leading tech giants, and there is currently no reason to believe it will lose significant ground over the next 1–3 years. Meanwhile, long-term investors should note that the company pays almost no dividends. The annual yield is approximately 0.022% or $0.04 per share. On January 25, 2026, Nvidia reported fiscal quarterly results that set records across multiple metrics. Total revenue reached $68.1 billion, representing a 73% year-over-year increase and marking a new quarterly high. The Data Center segment was the primary growth driver, with revenue rising 75% year-over-year to $62.3 billion, fueled by strong demand for AI infrastructure, GPUs, and data center computing platforms. Net income for the quarter totaled $43 billion, up 94% year-over-year. Performance across other segments remained stable. The gaming division continues to expand, although its share of total revenue is gradually declining. Meanwhile, the company’s automotive, engineering, and AI-driven solutions segments are steadily expanding. Some investors believe that NVDA stock has already captured most of its upside potential and that any further gains are likely to be more modest compared to previous years. This view is largely driven by intensifying competition, which could erode the company's market share and revenue growth. Supporters of this perspective argue that it may be prudent to lock in profits at current levels and reallocate capital toward competitors with stronger near-term growth prospects. Nvidia's stock price and returns over the past year: The slowdown in Nvidia's growth over the past year points to intensifying competition in the semiconductor and AI sectors. Although TSMC is not a direct competitor, the two companies operate within closely related segments of the industry. As a result, some investors may consider reallocating capital from NVDA into other sector players, including established blue-chip companies. In the US market, Nvidia's key competitors include Intel and Broadcom, while in the AI space, China's DeepSeek is also emerging as a notable player. Macroeconomic and market risks are key factors in shaping the external environment in which a company operates. Economic shifts, exchange rate fluctuations, inflation, and market volatility can significantly affect business performance and strategic decisions. Understanding and timely assessment of these factors allows investors to minimize potential losses and enhance business resilience. Economic slowdown and reduced IT spending. In the event of a global recession, companies may cut back on investments in data centers and AI infrastructure, directly reducing demand for Nvidia GPUs. Reduced customer dependence. Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta are developing their own AI processors to reduce their reliance on Nvidia. Geopolitical restrictions. US export restrictions on AI chip shipments to China could shrink one of the company's key markets. Dependence on supply chains. The technology is still in the early stages of development and is far from reaching full maturity. Despite the rapid integration of AI into everyday life, it is not yet capable of fully replacing human expertise in key roles, which suggests that companies will continue to invest heavily in technological advancement. As one of the industry leaders, Nvidia is well-positioned to benefit from this trend, with its solutions likely to remain in strong demand. Over the past year, Nvidia has announced a number of long-term initiatives in the field of AI: In March 2026, the company announced plans to invest $2 billion in Nebius (NBIS) to support the construction of AI-focused data centers. This initiative is part of a broader program to develop 5 GW of capacity by 2030. Nvidia remains a minority shareholder and has emphasized its openness to collaboration across the industry. The financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. In December 2025, the company formed a strategic partnership with Groq, a startup specializing in processors for accelerating neural networks. In a deal valued at $20 billion—the largest in Nvidia's history—the company gained access to Groq's technologies and key assets. In October 2025, Nvidia announced its plan to supply Samsung and Hyundai with 260,000 advanced processors. In September 2025, discussions were held regarding a potential $110 billion funding round for OpenAI ahead of a possible IPO. Nvidia was expected to contribute $30 billion, alongside Amazon ($50 billion) and SoftBank ($30 billion), to build large-scale AI data center infrastructure. These examples demonstrate that the company remains committed to maintaining and expanding its market share. Nvidia is a growth stock because the company is forming long-term strategic partnerships with major tech companies, indicating sustainable future growth. Nvidia is unlikely to lose ground to its rivals, and its stock is not expected to plummet in the near future. At the same time, the stock will unlikely surge by more than 1,000% over the next five years. Over the long term, the company's stock is projected to grow at a moderate pace of 30–50% annually. Meanwhile, risks cannot be ruled out. For example, an escalation of tensions around Taiwan—one of the key hubs of the global semiconductor industry—could represent a potential black swan event. At the same time, recent geopolitical developments have shown that Nvidia's stock has been relatively resilient to such shocks.
